svg.title: Three routing protocol families compared by mechanism, source of scalability and blind spot
svg.desc: Three columns. Link state, OSPF and IS-IS: flood the topology, every node runs SPF, scalability comes from hierarchy and summarization, and the blind spot is that every topology change is flooded across the area. Path vector, BGP: propagates paths rather than topology, scalability comes from policy control and trusting only neighbours, and the blind spot is that convergence follows policy, not topology. Distance vector and hybrid, RIP and EIGRP: propagates my distance to X, scalability comes from summarization and controlling the query scope, and the blind spot is that each router cannot see why the neighbour said that distance. A note at the bottom says link state buys fault localisation with flooding, distance vector buys quiet neighbours with blindness.

One sentence to separate them: in a link-state protocol every router knows the whole topology and computes paths itself;
in a distance-vector protocol every router only knows the distance its neighbour told it, and never asks why.
